title: Merge Intervals: Combine Everything That Overlaps
oneLiner: Sort by start time first, then a single left-to-right pass is enough to merge every overlapping interval -- no interval needs to be revisited once merged.
keyTakeaway: Once intervals are SORTED by start, an interval can only possibly overlap the current merged interval (everything earlier ends before it) -- so a single pass comparing each interval to the last one KEPT (not the last one seen) is enough; the sort is what makes one pass sufficient.
explanation:
Given a list of intervals, merge every pair that overlaps into one combined interval. The key insight: this is hard to do correctly on UNSORTED intervals (any interval could overlap any other), but trivial once they're SORTED by start time -- after sorting, if an interval doesn't overlap the interval immediately after it, it can't overlap anything further away either (since everything further away starts even later). That collapses the problem to one left-to-right pass.

Walk the sorted intervals one at a time, keeping a "current merged interval" (start with the first one). For each next interval: if its start is <= the current merged interval's end, they overlap -- extend the current merged interval's end to cover the larger of the two ends. If it doesn't overlap, the current merged interval is finished -- record it, and start a new current merged interval from this one.

Watch the sorted intervals collapse into fewer, wider ones below -- each interval only ever gets compared against the CURRENT merged result, never against every other interval, which is what keeps this an O(n log n) algorithm (dominated by the sort) instead of O(n^2).

recognitionSignals: The problem gives a list of ranges/intervals and asks you to combine, count, or find overlaps among them.
Any brute-force approach would compare every interval against every other interval (O(n^2)) -- sorting first should immediately come to mind.
gotchas: Whether touching endpoints count as overlapping ([1,4] and [4,5]) is a real ambiguity some problems specify explicitly -- using <= instead of < in the overlap check treats them as overlapping; double check which the problem wants.
Forgetting to sort first (or sorting by the wrong field, like end instead of start) breaks the single-pass guarantee entirely.
confusableWith: Sliding Window (this track) also processes a sequence in one pass, but slides a WINDOW of fixed or growing/shrinking size over an array; merging intervals compares each new interval only against the last MERGED result, not a moving window boundary.

complexity.note: Sorting by start dominates (n log n); the merge pass after it is a single O(n) sweep. The output list can hold up to n intervals.
